notes:
Below are notes on Hebrews 8, verse by verse. I had fewer searches than I'd have liked, so the sources lean on Precept Austin, Enduring Word, Bible Hub, StudyLight, Ligonier and Bible.org. The list of gaps at the end shows what I didn't find.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- This verse sums up the argument of chapter 7. Believers have a High Priest who is not bound to earthly rituals but is enthroned at God's right hand in heaven. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_81-3
- Guzik (Enduring Word) makes a point of the word "sat": the tabernacle and temple had no place for the priests to sit, because their work was never finished. Jesus' work is finished, so He is seated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-8/
- Barnes notes that the Greek word translated "sum" or "point" (kephalaion) is taken by many old and modern interpreters to mean the "principal thing," the most important point. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-8.html

**v. 2**
- Barnes says the "true tabernacle" means heaven, God's dwelling, of which the tabernacle Moses made was only the emblem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-8.html
- Guzik mentions that some take the true tabernacle to be the Church or Jesus' earthly body, but he thinks it best understood as the heavenly reality the earthly tabernacle copied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-8/
- Bible Hub's study notes say the Greek word for "minister" (leitourgos) means a public servant or one who performs religious duties. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/8.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: sacrifice for sin is essential to priesthood. Jesus offered a better sacrifice by laying down His own life to atone for sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-8/
- Matthew Henry: having finished the work of sacrifice on earth, Christ goes into heaven to present His righteousness and to intercede there. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_008.cfm
- Catholic and Protestant writers read this verse quite differently. See section 3.

**v. 4**
- Guthrie, quoted on Precept Austin, says the writer is clearing up a possible confusion about two priesthoods existing side by side. Jesus could not meet the Mosaic Law's conditions, either in ancestry or in the exact gifts required. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_84-6
- Steven Cole, citing Philip Hughes, says the present-tense wording here shows the temple was still standing, which dates Hebrews before AD 70. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-23-better-priest-better-covenant-hebrews-81-13

**v. 5**
- Precept Austin's summary: the priesthood and tabernacle did real service, but only in an earthly model pointing to the heavenly reality. Christ's ministry is the substance itself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_84-6
- Barnes says the word translated "warned" (chrēmatizō) properly means to give an oracle, a message from God by dream or direct revelation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-8.html
- Guzik notes that at least four Old Testament passages say the tabernacle was built "according to the pattern" God gave Moses. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/how-many-temples-were-built-in-jerusalem-qa-with-david-guzik/

**v. 6**
- Wuest calls this a pivotal verse that closes the letter's first major argument. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/hebrews_84-6
- Vincent's word studies: in Hebrews the sanctuary and the covenant belong together, because God's covenant was embodied in the sanctuary. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/hebrews_84-6
- Guzik describes the better covenant as marked by believing and receiving instead of earning and deserving. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-8/

**v. 7**
- Precept Austin says this verse does not run down God's law. It shows the law's limits: it could not produce inward change or lasting forgiveness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_87-9
- Mathison (Ligonier) says the new covenant was not God's "plan B." Both covenants were part of God's plan from the beginning, each suited to its time. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/new-covenant

**v. 8**
- The usual reading is that the fault lay with the people. The main problem was not the covenant itself but the people's failure to keep it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_87-9
- Barnes records an older disagreement. Some take the fault to be with the covenant itself rather than the people. Grotius and Erasmus read it that way, while Doddridge and others say the fault was with the people. Barnes himself concludes that the point is simply that there was a lack, which the new covenant would remove. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-8.html
- Guzik: at Sinai the key words were "if you"; in the new covenant they are "I will." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-8/
- Whether "Israel and Judah" means the church or ethnic Israel is disputed. See section 2.

**v. 9**
- Guzik: the weakness was not in the covenant but in human weakness and inability. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-8/
- Henry sees in "took them by the hand" God's great affection, condescension and tender care. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_008.cfm
- A text note: Hebrews follows the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) here. Cole says the Hebrew reads "although I was a husband to them," and the difference may come from a one-letter variation. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-24-better-covenant-hebrews-87-12

**v. 10**
- Henry: God once wrote His laws to them; now He will write His laws in them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_008.cfm
- Barnes: the law is written on the soul itself, not on stone, so obedience will not be merely outward. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-8.html
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "The best way to make a man keep a law is to make him love the law-giver." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-8/
- Cole stresses that this inner change is a process and is not complete until Christ returns. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-24-better-covenant-hebrews-87-12

**v. 11**
- Cole: most people under the Sinai covenant did not personally know God, but under the new covenant all of God's people receive the Spirit, which he sees as the fulfilment of "all will know Me." https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-24-better-covenant-hebrews-87-12

**v. 12**
- Barnes: "remember no more" is spoken in human terms. God does not literally forget, but treats people as if their sins were forgotten. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-8.html
- Another commentator on Precept Austin says the phrase means "hold against us no more." https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_812-13
- Meyer argues that forgiveness is fundamental to any renewal of covenant. Another Bible Hub commentator says the earlier promises flow from this final one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/8-12.htm
- Trapp: if we remember our sins with grief and bring them to confession, God will forget them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/heb-8.cfm

**v. 13**
- Precept Austin: the old covenant was not evil but temporary, meant to point forward to Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_812-13
- Bible Hub notes the temple was still standing when Hebrews was written, and that its destruction by Rome in AD 70 underlines the warning that what is aging will soon disappear. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/8.htm

## 2. Where Protestants differ

These differences follow theological systems rather than denominations.

**vv. 8–10: who is "the house of Israel"?**
- **Reformed, covenant theology:** Mathison (Ligonier) says "My laws" in v. 10 shows continuity between the covenants. The moral law stays the same; it is now written on hearts instead of stone. He also writes that God's people are now defined by their relation to Jesus, not to Jacob. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/new-covenant
- A Ligonier devotional adds that old covenant believers had the benefits of the new covenant, though to a lesser degree. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-promised-new-covenant
- Walvoord, a dispensationalist writing on Bible.org, describes the amillennial Reformed view (Allis) this way: it identifies Israel with the church and applies the new covenant promises to believing Jews and Gentiles now. https://bible.org/seriespage/18-new-covenant-israel
- Henry, an older Nonconformist, already took "Israel" as all the Israel of God. Barnes takes it as God's people in general. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_008.cfm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/hebrews-8.html
- **Classic dispensational:** Darby held the new covenant was made with Israel and Judah, not the church, and would be fulfilled later. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/shirley_dave/HoR/HoR18.cfm
- William Newell says this new covenant with Israel is still future, in the Millennium. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews-verse-by-verse-2
- **Double fulfilment, a mediating dispensational view:** the Believer's Study Bible says the covenant applies to two groups: the church now, and national Israel in the millennial age. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_810-11
- **Cole, a Baptist pastor:** he rejects both full covenant theology and the "two new covenants" view. He says the church shares in the one new covenant Jeremiah foretold, with a future revival among the Jews still to come. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-24-better-covenant-hebrews-87-12

**v. 13: continuity or a clean break?**
- Mathison warns against two extremes: saying nothing in the Old Testament applies to Christians, and treating the changes as cosmetic (for example, insisting on a seventh-day Sabbath). https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/new-covenant
- One Precept Austin commentator applies the verse as a warning to Christians not to put themselves back under the law. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/hebrews_812-13

## 3. Other views

**v. 3, Catholic reading:** Catholic Answers argues that because Christ's one sacrifice culminated in glory, He continues to offer it in the heavenly sanctuary (citing Heb. 8:1–3). On this view the Mass is not a new sin offering but a fresh participation in Christ's one sacrifice of Calvary. https://www.catholic.com/qa/why-the-mass-when-theres-no-need-for-sin-offering
- Another Catholic Answers piece says Christ's heavenly ministry re-presents His single sacrifice to the Father as a memorial offering. It denies that Christ dies repeatedly. https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/the-one-and-only-sacrifice-of-the-mass
- The same site sums up the disagreement: "Protestants say 'one and done.' Catholics say the sacrifice continues forever." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/when-did-jesus-finish-his-sacrifice
- For the Protestant side, Guzik reads Christ's being seated as a sign of finished work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-8/

**v. 12, popular devotional uses:** Precept Austin collects short devotional takes on this verse. Charles Stanley says perfect performance isn't possible in this life and God doesn't require it. Adrian Rogers, on the other hand, ties forgiveness to confession: "I confess it; I put it under the blood." https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_812-13

## Not found
I found nothing specific to Hebrews 8 from Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Anglican or Orthodox teachers. The Wesley page I found had only the verse text, no notes. I also found no NET Bible or Bible Odyssey scholarship, and no source that discusses prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
